title: Ahaz: The King Who Sought Every Help but God's
summary: Ahaz walks in the ways of Israel's kings, makes images of the Baals, and burns his sons in the fire in the Valley of Hinnom. Judah is devastated by Aram and by Israel, whose army takes two hundred thousand captives until the prophet Oded persuades the leaders of Samaria to clothe, feed, and return them. Ahaz turns to Assyria for help, strips the temple to pay for it, sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, and finally shuts the doors of the house of the LORD.
story: After Jotham's quiet faithfulness, his son Ahaz plunges Judah to its lowest point so far. Chronicles tells his reign as a series of disasters that the king meets by reaching for every source of help except the LORD. The surprise in the middle is that the most godly people in the chapter are northerners: a prophet and a group of leaders in Samaria who show mercy to their Judean kinsmen. The chapter ends with the temple doors closed, which sets the stage for the next four chapters, where Hezekiah's first act is to open them again. Judah's story in Chronicles now moves toward its final pattern: collapse, reform, collapse again.
historical:
Ahaz reigned in the second half of the eighth century BC; a common reconstruction dates his rule to about 735 to 715 BC, though the chronology of this period is much debated. The parallel is 2 Kings 16, and Isaiah 7 tells of the prophet's meeting with Ahaz during the same crisis. Around 734 BC, Rezin king of Aram and Pekah king of Israel attacked Judah, probably to force it into a coalition against Assyria. Ahaz appealed to Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria, who crushed Damascus in 732 BC and annexed much of the northern kingdom's territory. Assyrian royal inscriptions from Tiglath-pileser's reign list Ahaz, under his fuller name Jehoahaz, among the western kings who paid him tribute.

At the same time Edom and the Philistines seized Judah's weakness to raid the south and the lowlands (verses 17-18). Within a few years of Ahaz's death the northern kingdom itself would fall to Assyria in 722 BC, a fact that stands behind the prophet Oded's warning that Israel's own guilt was great.
cultural:
Burning children "in the fire" in the Valley of Hinnom, just south of Jerusalem, was a practice the Law condemned as one of the abominations of the nations (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 18:10). It was associated with the god Molech and with rites performed in times of desperate crisis. The valley's Hebrew name, Ge-Hinnom, later became Gehenna, the word Jesus used for the place of final judgment.

Sending tribute to a great king was how a small kingdom bought protection in the Assyrian age, but the protection came at the price of vassal status, annual payments, and often religious and political pressure. Ahaz's logic in verse 23, sacrificing to the gods of Damascus because they seemed to have helped Aram, reflects the common belief that a nation's success showed the power of its gods. The kindness of the Samarian leaders in verse 15 was striking in a world where war captives were routinely enslaved: they clothe, shoe, feed, anoint, and carry the weak on donkeys to Jericho.
literary: The word help runs through the chapter like a thread. Ahaz sends to Assyria "for help" (verse 16), but the Assyrian king "did not help him" (verse 21), and he sacrifices to Aram's gods so "that they may help me" (verse 23), only for them to become his downfall. The narrator's verdicts are placed between the events: because they had forsaken the LORD (verse 6), because Ahaz had been most unfaithful (verse 19). The Oded episode (verses 9-15) is a deliberate interlude that reverses expectations. Judah's king is faithless, while leaders in apostate Samaria confess their guilt and obey a prophet. The Chronicler also calls Ahaz "king of Israel" in verse 19, a reminder that for him Israel names the whole covenant people, not only the northern kingdom.

outline.t: Oded's rebuke and the return of the captives
Ahaz seeks Assyria's help and is afflicted instead
Deeper unfaithfulness and the closing of the temple
Death and burial outside the royal tombs

doctrines.note: Ahaz's idolatry is a search for help in the wrong places. He tries Baal, the high places, Assyria's king, and Damascus's gods. Each promises security and each fails, which is the Bible's steady diagnosis of idols.
The leaders of Samaria hear the prophet, confess that their own guilt is great, and act to undo a wrong. Repentance appears where it is least expected and is shown in concrete mercy, not only words.

God's judgment on Judah comes through foreign armies, yet the prophet warns the victors that they too stand under judgment for their cruelty. Being used as an instrument of discipline does not make anyone righteous.

words.note: Azar, to help. It is the chapter's ironic key word. Earlier in Chronicles God helped faithful kings (Uzziah in 26:7 and 26:15). Ahaz seeks help from Assyria and from foreign gods, and the text says plainly that none of it helped him.

Ashmah, guilt. It appears four times in Oded's speech and the leaders' reply (verses 10 and 13). Their confession, that their guilt is great, stands in sharp contrast to Ahaz, who never admits anything.
Maal, to be unfaithful. Used of Uzziah's trespass in chapter 26, it now describes Ahaz three times (verses 19 and 22). His unfaithfulness grows in distress rather than driving him back to God.

christ: Readers have long noticed how closely the scene in verse 15 resembles Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30-37): people from Samaria clothe the naked, anoint wounds, set the weak on donkeys, and bring them to Jericho. Whether Jesus intended an echo is debated, but the shared picture is clear: mercy shown across the hostile line between Judah and Samaria. Ahaz's reign also stands behind one of the most famous promises in the Old Testament. When Ahaz refused to trust God during this war, Isaiah gave him the sign of a child called Immanuel, God with us (Isaiah 7:14), which Matthew applies to the birth of Jesus (Matthew 1:23). The king who shut the temple doors was offered the presence of God himself and did not want it.

hard.q: 2 Kings 16:9 says the Assyrian king heeded Ahaz and captured Damascus, but verse 20 here says he afflicted Ahaz rather than strengthening him. Which is right?
hard.a: Both accounts can stand together. Kings reports the immediate military result: Assyria attacked Damascus and killed Rezin, removing one enemy. Chronicles reports the long-term cost: Ahaz became a vassal, emptied the temple and palace to pay tribute, and gained no lasting security, since Edom and Philistia still raided Judah and Assyria's demands continued. Some scholars see the Chronicler as reshaping Kings to make a theological point about misplaced trust; others see the two books as describing different aspects of the same events. Either way, the Chronicler's claim is that the help Ahaz bought was not help at all.

questions: Ahaz tried one source of help after another. Where do you turn first when you feel threatened, and what does that reveal about what you trust?
The leaders in Samaria obeyed a prophet and showed mercy to their enemies. Who are the unexpected people whose obedience has shamed or taught you?
In his distress Ahaz became more unfaithful, not less. How can suffering drive a person away from God, and what helps it drive them toward him instead?
